title: Recommendations on the preparation of silicon solar cell samples for defect etching
author: Pacho, Rinio

steps.title: Mount sample securely on holder
steps.instruction: Place the 25 mm × 25 mm mc‑Si solar cell on the polishing holder, ensuring full contact, no air bubbles or gaps, and secure it firmly.

steps.title: Clean equipment before grinding
steps.instruction: Rinse the polishing cloth, holder, and sample with deionized water, dry them, and remove any debris before the first grinding step.

steps.title: Grind with SiC 1200‑grit
steps.instruction: Use SiC 1200‑grit (Struers) with water as slurry; set disk rotation to 300 rpm, sample rotation to 150 rpm, apply 5 N force, and process for 1 min.

steps.title: Clean and inspect after grinding
steps.instruction: Thoroughly clean the sample and polishing cloth, then inspect the surface under an optical microscope for scratches; repeat cleaning if debris remains.

steps.title: Grind with SiC 2000‑grit
steps.instruction: Use SiC 2000‑grit (Struers) with water slurry; keep disk at 300 rpm, sample at 150 rpm, force 5 N, and run for 1 min.

steps.title: Clean and inspect after grinding
steps.instruction: Rinse and dry the sample and cloth, then examine the surface for uniformity and absence of deep scratches.

steps.title: Polish with 9 µm diamond
steps.instruction: Place Taffeta woven wool (Struers MD‑Mol) on the holder, apply Diamond suspension – 9 µm (Struers DiaPro Plan 9 µm); rotate both disk and sample at 150 rpm, apply 10 N force, and polish for 3 min.

steps.title: Clean and inspect after polishing
steps.instruction: Clean the sample and the Taffeta cloth, then inspect the surface for residual scratches before proceeding.

steps.title: Polish with 3 µm diamond
steps.instruction: Use Taffeta woven wool (Struers MD‑Mol) with Diamond suspension – 3 µm (Struers DiaPro Mol B 3 µm); keep both rotations at 150 rpm, force 10 N, and polish for 5 min.

steps.title: Clean and inspect after polishing
steps.instruction: Rinse and dry the sample and cloth, then verify under a microscope that scratches from the previous step are removed.

steps.title: Polish with 1 µm diamond
steps.instruction: Place Synthetic nap textile (Struers MD‑Nap) on the holder, apply Diamond suspension – 1 µm (Struers DiaPro Nap B 1 µm); rotate both at 150 rpm, apply 10 N force, and polish for 5 min.

steps.title: Clean and inspect after polishing
steps.instruction: Clean the sample and nap textile thoroughly, then inspect the surface to ensure it is free of scratches before the final step.

steps.title: Chemical‑mechanical polish with colloidal silica
steps.instruction: Use Poromeric pad (Eminess Politex reg) with Colloidal Silica – 0.09 µm, pH 11.9 (Eminess Ultra‑Sol 558); rotate disk and sample at 150 rpm, apply 20 N force, and process for 15 min.

steps.title: Final clean and inspection
steps.instruction: Rinse the polished sample, dry it, and perform a final microscopic inspection to confirm a scratch‑free surface ready for defect etching.

description: The polishing method presented in this work has been used to prepare mc-Si solar cells for Secco etching. The etched samples were imaged using an optical microscope with a moveable stage at a resolution of about 0.34 µm/pixel. A typical result is presented in Fig. 5 where a grid of 7 × 7 individual microscope images are stitched together after performing shading correction. This method has been successfully employed in analyzing the images of etched samples and correlating them with internal quantum efficiency measurements using light beam induced current to quantify the impact of grain boundaries on the performance of mc-Si solar cells [10].Fig. 5A stitched image of 7 × 7 images of a sample after polishing and etching. The brightness and contrast of the image was adjusted after performing shading correction to improve visibility.Fig 5 Proper sample preparation prior to defect etching is paramount to simpler and more efficient imaging and image analysis. Polishing a batch of samples, despite the short processing times listed in Table 1, can easily take up a whole working day since a significant amount of work must be done before processing and in between steps. The temptation to quicken the pace must be moderated by the fact that correcting for polishing artifacts like scratches in the etched sample, i.e. by manually deleting them in the images or adjusting the image analysis algorithm to disregard them, can be more time consuming and tedious. Mounting samples securely is the first and foremost protection for the samples. Cracks, edge chipping and sample breakages can be minimized with proper sample mounting. Having air bubbles or a significant gap between the sample and the sample holder is another important thing that is easy to overlook. Abrasives and polishing slurry can get trapped in between this gap and contaminate the cloth for the next polishing step, causing unintended scratches for that step despite the precautions taken to avoid cloth contamination.
